Earth's Interior, Rocks and Plate Tectonics
One theory explains quakes, mountains and oceans

Almost every physical-geography question in GS I leads back to plate tectonics . Earthquakes, volcanoes, fold mountains, ocean trenches and even the shape of India all follow from it. To answer well you need three things: what is inside the Earth, how we know, and how plates move. We take them in that order.
The layered Earth

We cannot drill beyond about 12 km. So scientists use indirect evidence: seismic waves , meteorites, gravity, magnetism and density. Crust is thin under oceans (about 5 km, basalt, called sima) and thick under continents (about 30 km, granite, called sial).
Discontinuities: where the layers change

A discontinuity is a boundary where seismic waves change speed or direction. The Moho was found in 1909 by the Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovicic. Know the pairs above: Moho, Gutenberg, Lehmann.
Seismic waves and the liquid core

P waves are primary, fast and longitudinal. S waves are secondary and transverse, and cannot pass through liquid. L waves travel on the surface and do the most damage. S waves vanish at the core. This proved the outer core is liquid.
Three rock families

Igneous rocks form from cooled magma. Intrusive ones such as granite cool slowly; extrusive ones such as basalt cool fast. Sedimentary rocks form from compacted sediments, often with fossils and layers, e.g. sandstone and limestone. Metamorphic rocks are changed by heat or pressure, e.g. marble from limestone and slate from shale.
Wegener and continental drift, 1912

Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912, and published in 1915, that all land once formed one supercontinent, Pangaea , in the ocean Panthalassa. It broke up about 200 million years ago. His evidence: the jigsaw fit of Africa and South America, matching rocks and fossils (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris), and glacial deposits across southern continents. His weakness: he could not explain the force that moved continents. Geologists rejected him.
Sea-floor spreading

In the early 1960s Harry Hess argued that new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and spreads outward. Old crust sinks at trenches. Vine and Matthews (1963) found symmetrical magnetic stripes on either side of a ridge, recording reversals of Earth's field. Ocean floor is young: nowhere older than about 180 million years. Continents hold rocks over 4 billion years old.
Plate tectonics, late 1960s

The theory was assembled by McKenzie, Parker and Morgan (1967-68). The lithosphere (crust plus top mantle) is broken into 7 major plates (Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic) and many minor ones. Plates float on the soft asthenosphere .
What drives the plates?

Three ideas compete and probably work together: mantle convection (hot rock rising, cold sinking), slab pull (a heavy sinking plate drags the rest, thought to be strongest) and ridge push . Hotspots are fixed plumes in the mantle. Plates drift over them and leave volcanic chains, e.g. Hawaii. Critics note that the plume idea is still debated, and that the exact driving force is not fully settled.
India as a travelling plate

The Indian plate split from Gondwana and moved north at up to 15-20 cm a year before colliding with Eurasia about 50 million years ago. It still pushes at about 5 cm a year. This built the Himalaya , which is why they still rise and shake. Passing over the Reunion hotspot , India erupted the Deccan Traps about 66 million years ago. Subduction under Myanmar causes the Andaman volcanoes, including Barren Island, India's only active volcano.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the theory of plate tectonics and its role in explaining earthquakes and volcanoes." (15 marks) "How did the Himalaya form?" (10 marks) Structure: start with Wegener and Hess as the roots; give the plate idea; draw the three boundaries; link each to landforms; end with India's collision zone. Prelims tip: know which waves cannot pass through liquid (S), the depth of the Gutenberg discontinuity, and that the Indo-Australian plate is a single major plate in the usual list.
Earthquakes, Volcanoes and Tsunamis
The Earth moves, and people die

Quakes, volcanoes and tsunamis appear both in Physical Geography and in disaster management. India has had Latur (1993), Bhuj (2001), the 2004 tsunami and Nepal (2015). UPSC asks about causes, distribution and India's exposure.
How an earthquake works

Stress builds on a fault. Rock slips, and energy spreads as waves. Magnitude (Richter, now usually the moment scale) is logarithmic: each step is about 10 times the wave amplitude and about 32 times the energy. Intensity (Mercalli, I to XII) measures effects felt.
Where quakes strike
Quakes mostly follow plate boundaries. Shallow quakes happen at all boundaries. Deep ones only occur in subduction zones. Intraplate quakes (Latur, Bhuj) are rarer, along old buried faults.
Causes beyond plates

Volcanic quakes, collapse quakes (mines, caves) and reservoir-induced quakes also occur. The Koyna quake of 1967 (about M6.3) is the classic Indian case of reservoir-induced seismicity. Effects: ground shaking, liquefaction, landslides, fires, tsunamis. The shaking and poor building, not the quake itself, kills most people.
Volcanoes and their forms

A volcano is a vent where magma reaches the surface. Shield volcanoes (Mauna Loa) are broad with runny basalt. Composite cones (Fuji, Vesuvius) alternate lava and ash and are explosive. Caldera (Krakatoa, Toba) forms when a cone collapses. Flood basalts built the Deccan Traps.
Intrusive and extrusive forms

Magma cooling underground makes batholiths (big domes), laccoliths (lens with a flat base), sills (horizontal sheets) and dykes (vertical walls). Dykes are common in the Deccan. Surface forms include cones, lava plateaus and geysers and hot springs from heated ground water. Volcano status: active, dormant or extinct.
Tsunami

A tsunami (Japanese for harbour wave) is a series of waves from a sudden seabed shift, usually from a subduction quake, landslide or eruption. It is hardly seen in deep water. On reaching shallows it slows and rises. Hunga Tonga (2022) showed that eruptions can cause them too.
India's seismic map and the 2004 tsunami

The long-used BIS map (IS 1893, 2002) has four zones, II to V, with Zone V the highest. About 59% of India's land is quake-prone. A revised BIS code released in November 2025 adds a new Zone VI for the Himalayan arc, so check which map a question refers to. On 26 December 2004 a magnitude 9.1-9.3 quake off Sumatra sent waves to Tamil Nadu, Andhra, Kerala and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. India then set up the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre at INCOIS, Hyderabad (2007).
Can we predict earthquakes?

No. Science can give probabilities and hazard maps, not exact times. Early-warning systems exploit the gap between fast P waves and damaging S waves, giving seconds of notice. Real risk reduction comes from building codes , retrofitting, land-use rules and drills. After Bhuj (26 January 2001, M7.7) and Nepal (25 April 2015, M7.8) the debate shifted from nature to unsafe construction.
How to write this

Likely questions "Describe the distribution of volcanoes and earthquakes in the world." (10 marks) "Why is the Himalayan region prone to earthquakes? How do they differ from the Peninsular ones?" (15 marks) Structure: define; give causes; map the Pacific and Alpine belts; add Indian zones; end with mitigation (codes, early warning, drills). Prelims tip: Richter is logarithmic; Mercalli measures intensity; Barren Island is India's only active volcano; Koyna is the reservoir-induced example.
Landforms and Geomorphic Processes
Landforms are the Earth's fingerprints

Every hill, delta and dune is the result of a tug of war between forces that build land and forces that wear it down. GS I asks for this reasoning, often through Indian examples such as ravines, karst or the Sundarbans.
Endogenic and exogenic forces

Endogenic forces (volcanism, folding, faulting) create relief. Exogenic forces (weathering, erosion, transport, deposition) reduce it. Landforms are the net result. Sudden endogenic events are earthquakes and volcanoes; slow ones are mountain building and warping.
Weathering and mass movement

Weathering breaks rock in place, with no transport. Physical (frost, exfoliation from day-night heating), chemical (oxidation, carbonation, solution) and biological types act together. Warm, wet climates favour chemical action, giving thick soils and laterite . Mass movement is the downslope shift of material under gravity: creep, flow, slide, fall. Heavy rain, steep slopes and cut roads trigger Himalayan landslides.
Running water: the strongest agent

Rivers cut valleys upstream and deposit downstream. Key forms: waterfalls (Jog on the Sharavati, Hogenakkal), meanders, oxbow lakes, alluvial fans where a river leaves hills, and deltas where it meets the sea. Rivers hit by a base-level fall or uplift cut deep gorges.
Glaciers

Ice cuts U-shaped valleys , scoops cirques , and leaves sharp arete ridges and pyramid horns (Matterhorn). It dumps moraines , and shapes drumlins and eskers . Siachen, Gangotri and Zemu are Indian glaciers. Kumaon-Garhwal glacial lakes and "hanging valleys" are common.
Wind, groundwater and sea

Wind works in dry lands: deflation hollows, mushroom rocks, yardangs, crescent barchans and fine loess deposits (China). Groundwater in limestone makes karst : sinkholes, caves, stalactites. Waves build cliffs, stacks, spits and bars, and form beaches.
Major relief types

Mountains: fold (Himalaya, Alps), block or horst (Vosges, Black Forest), volcanic (Fuji), and residual or relict (Aravalli, Nilgiri). Plateaus: intermontane (Tibet), piedmont and continental (Deccan). Plains: erosional (peneplain) and depositional (Indo-Gangetic, alluvial). The Aravalli are among the oldest fold ranges, now worn down. The Rift valley of the Narmada and Tapi is a down-faulted block, a graben.
Davis, Penck and the cycle of erosion

W.M. Davis (1899) proposed a "cycle": uplift, then youth, maturity and old age ending in a flat peneplain. Walther Penck (1924) argued uplift and erosion work together, so slopes retreat in parallel. Critics say Davis assumed a quick uplift followed by a calm period. Modern geomorphology favours dynamic equilibrium and human activity as a driver: mining, dams and farming now move more earth than many rivers.
Indian landforms at a glance

Ravines and badlands: Chambal and Yamuna, formed by gully erosion in soft alluvium. Barchans: Thar. Karst: Meghalaya (Mawsmai and Krem Liat Prah caves), Chhattisgarh (Kutumsar) and Borra caves in Andhra Pradesh. Delta: Ganga-Brahmaputra, the world's largest, with the Sundarbans mangroves. Coastal erosion eats Kerala's shores. Himalayan landslides, as at Joshimath (2023, subsidence), show human pressure on fragile slopes.
How to write this

Likely questions "Explain the role of running water in shaping the Indian landscape." (10 marks) "Differentiate between weathering, erosion and mass wasting." (10 marks) Structure: split into endogenic and exogenic; then agent by agent, with a landform and an Indian example each. Prelims tip: know the agent behind each landform (U-valley = glacier, barchan = wind, stalactite = groundwater, oxbow = river).
Atmosphere, Insolation and Heat Budget
Climate begins with the sun
Monsoon, deserts, cyclones and global warming all start with one question: how much solar energy reaches a place, and where does it go? The heat budget is the answer and a UPSC favourite.
What air is made of

Dry air by volume: nitrogen 78% , oxygen 21% , argon 0.93%, carbon dioxide about 0.04% (over 420 ppm as of the mid-2020s, rising). Water vapour varies from 0 to 4%. Dust, salt and pollen act as hygroscopic nuclei for cloud formation. Gases are held by gravity. About 99% of air lies within 32 km of the ground.
Layers of the atmosphere

Boundaries are called pauses : tropopause, stratopause and so on. The tropopause is higher at the equator (about 18 km) than at the poles (about 8 km). Weather happens only in the troposphere. The ozone layer sits at 15 to 35 km.
Insolation: what controls it

Insolation is incoming solar radiation, mostly short-wave. It depends on: the angle of rays (equator gets near-vertical rays), length of day , the transparency of air (clouds, dust), and the Sun-Earth distance. Earth is nearest the Sun ( perihelion ) in early January and farthest ( aphelion ) in early July. Season, not distance, makes summer and winter, because Earth's axis is tilted by 23.5 degrees.
The heat budget
Earth neither heats up nor cools down overall, so incoming and outgoing energy balance. Greenhouse gases keep the average surface near 15 C instead of about -18 C.
How heat moves

Conduction : contact, mostly at the ground. Convection : vertical air currents. Advection : horizontal movement, which is more important in weather, e.g. the hot dry Loo of north India. Latent heat : heat released when vapour condenses, which fuels cyclones.
Lapse rate and inversion
Inversions form on long, clear, calm winter nights with snow cover. They trap smoke in valleys. Mountain-side inversions favour orchards mid-slope because cold air drains downhill.
Greenhouse effect: natural versus enhanced

The natural effect is useful. Human burning of fossil fuels adds CO2 and methane, thickening the blanket. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to hold warming well below 2 C and pursue 1.5 C. Critics note that India, with low per capita emissions, argues for common but differentiated responsibilities . Ozone depletion is a separate problem: the Montreal Protocol (1987) phases out CFCs; the Kigali Amendment (2016) phases down HFCs.
Indian examples

The Tropic of Cancer passes through eight states (Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram). The Loo, pre-monsoon heat waves (IMD flags them above 40 C in plains) and Delhi winter smog from inversions and stubble burning all follow from this lesson. The Indo-Gangetic Plain is one of the world's most polluted air basins.
How to write this

Likely questions "Explain the heat budget of the Earth." (10 marks) "What is temperature inversion? Discuss its effects." (10 marks) Structure: define; draw the 100-unit diagram; explain the balance; link to greenhouse warming; give an Indian example. Prelims tip: ozone is in the stratosphere; the ionosphere reflects radio waves; the tropopause is highest at the equator; albedo is 35%.
Pressure Belts, Winds and Jet Streams
Why the wind blows where it does
Pressure differences drive winds. Winds move heat, moisture and cyclones, and shape rainfall from the Sahara to the Ganga. The Indian monsoon is simply a seasonal swing of this global system.
Pressure belts

Pressure rises where air sinks and falls where air rises. Thermal causes explain the equatorial low and polar highs. Dynamic causes (Earth's spin, sinking air) explain the subtropical highs and subpolar lows. Belts shift north and south with the Sun, about 5 to 10 degrees.
Coriolis force and wind direction

Earth's rotation deflects moving air to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern ( Ferrel's law ). The force is zero at the equator and greatest at the poles. Winds are named by where they come from. A westerly comes from the west. Winds blow from high to low pressure, and the closer the isobars, the stronger the wind.
Planetary winds

Trade winds blow towards the equator and carry steady weather. Westerlies are strong and stormy in the southern oceans: Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties, Screaming Sixties. Polar easterlies are cold and dry.
Three-cell model
At the ITCZ (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone) trades from both hemispheres meet and rise, forming huge cloud and rain bands. Its seasonal shift north over India is central to the monsoon.
Jet streams
Jets sit just below the tropopause, where air temperature contrasts are sharp.
Local winds

Land and sea breeze : day sea breeze, night land breeze. Valley and mountain winds . Katabatic : cold air draining downslope. Foehn (Alps) and Chinook (Rockies): warm, dry downslope winds that melt snow. Mistral : cold, from the Alps to the Mediterranean. Harmattan : dry dust wind from the Sahara.
Is the jet stream weakening?

Some studies link a warming Arctic to a wavier polar jet, with longer cold spells and heat domes. Others find the evidence mixed. The safe exam position: it is a research debate, but jets clearly shape extremes such as western disturbances and heat waves.
Jets and Indian weather

In winter the subtropical westerly jet shifts south of the Himalaya and steers western disturbances , giving rain and snow in the north-west (good for rabi wheat). In summer it moves north of the Tibetan plateau and the tropical easterly jet helps the burst of the monsoon. Local winds: Loo in north India, Kalbaisakhi (Nor'wester) in Bengal, Mango showers in Kerala and Karnataka.
How to write this

Likely questions "What are jet streams and how do they affect the weather and climate of India?" (10 marks) "Explain the general circulation of the atmosphere." (15 marks) Structure: pressure belts with cause; the three cells; winds; jets; then India (western disturbances, monsoon burst). Prelims tip: the tropical easterly jet is a summer feature; Ferrel's law gives right deflection in the northern hemisphere; Chinook is in North America.
Clouds, Precipitation and Cyclones
Cyclones kill and clouds feed

Rain feeds farms; cyclones destroy them. The same physics of rising moist air gives both. UPSC asks about types of rainfall, cyclone formation and India's cyclone record, often as short 10-mark questions.
Humidity, dew point and condensation

Absolute humidity is vapour weight per volume. Relative humidity is the percentage of what the air could hold at that temperature. When air cools to its dew point it is saturated and condenses on nuclei. Clouds are tiny water drops or ice crystals. Warm air holds more vapour. Cooling happens by rising, by contact with cold surfaces, or by mixing.
Clouds
Remember: cirro = high, alto = middle, strato = layered, cumulo = heaped, nimbo = rain-bearing.
Three kinds of rainfall

Convectional : heated ground, rising moist air, afternoon showers in the tropics. Orographic : air forced up a mountain. Cyclonic or frontal : air lifted along a front or a low-pressure centre. Hail forms in strong updraughts in cumulonimbus.
How a tropical cyclone forms

Conditions: sea surface above about 26.5 C , high humidity, a small-scale disturbance, low vertical wind shear and a Coriolis force strong enough (more than about 5 degrees from the equator). Heat from condensing vapour feeds the storm.
Naming and classification

Names are given by regional bodies. For the north Indian Ocean the RSMC at IMD, New Delhi assigns names from lists supplied by member countries (since 2004). Storm surge, not wind, causes most deaths.
Tropical and temperate cyclones
Temperate cyclones form where warm and cold air meet along a front . The cold front overtakes the warm front and the system occludes . Western disturbances are the Indian version.
India's cyclone record

Eastern coast (Bay of Bengal) gets more and stronger cyclones, mostly in October to November and April to May. Landfalls: Odisha super cyclone (1999), Phailin (2013), Fani (2019), Amphan (2020). The Arabian Sea has become more active: Tauktae (2021), Biparjoy (2023). Odisha's early warning and mass evacuation cut deaths from tens of thousands in 1999 to under 50 in Phailin, a model for the world.
Is climate change making cyclones worse?

Warmer seas add fuel. Studies suggest more intense storms and rapid intensification , especially in the Arabian Sea, though total numbers may not rise. Rising sea levels worsen surge flooding. The sound answer: intensity and rainfall likely increase; frequency is uncertain.
How to write this

Likely questions "Why are tropical cyclones more frequent in the Bay of Bengal than in the Arabian Sea?" (10 marks) "Differentiate between tropical and temperate cyclones." (10 marks) Structure: conditions; mechanism; classification; Indian cases; then mitigation (early warning, shelters, mangroves). Prelims tip: a cyclone does not form on the equator; RSMC New Delhi names north Indian Ocean storms; the eye is calm.
Climate Types and El Niño
Climate is not just weather

Weather is what happens today. Climate is the average over about 30 years. Classifying climates gives a language for vegetation, farming and settlement. El Nino explains why some monsoons fail. Both are everyday GS I questions.
Koppen's scheme

Wladimir Koppen (first version 1884, revised 1918 and 1936) used temperature, rainfall and natural vegetation. Small letters add detail: f wet all year, w dry winter, s dry summer, h hot, k cold. Highland climates are labelled H.
Tropical climates: A

Af equatorial: rain every day, dense forest (Amazon, Congo). Am monsoon: short dry spell (Kerala, Bangladesh). Aw savanna: dry winter, grass and scattered trees (Sudan, Brazilian campos, most of peninsular India). Annual temperature range is small near the equator; diurnal range is bigger than annual range.
Dry and temperate climates: B and C

BWh hot desert (Sahara, Thar) at about 30 degrees on west coasts where cold currents add dryness. BS steppe is the grassy fringe. Cs Mediterranean: wet winters, dry summers (California, Chile, Cape). Cfa China type: humid subtropical. Cfb British type: mild, rain all year, on west coasts at 40-60 degrees.
Cold and polar: D and E

Df cold with year-round precipitation: Siberia and Canada, the coniferous taiga . Winter is very long and the annual range of temperature is the largest on Earth. ET tundra and EF ice cap. Permafrost thaw is now a climate worry.
El Nino and the Walker circulation

El Nino is unusual warming of the central and eastern Pacific, first noticed off Peru near Christmas (el nino means the boy child). The paired atmospheric change is the Southern Oscillation, so together they are ENSO .
ENSO and the Indian Ocean Dipole

La Nina brings the reverse. India's monsoon is often weak in El Nino years (2002, 2009, 2014, 2015) but not always: 1997 was normal. A positive IOD can offset El Nino, as in 2019 with a strong positive IOD.
Is climate prediction a gamble?

ENSO is now forecast months ahead, helping farmers and the government stock grain. But the link to India is not one-to-one, because the IOD, the Madden-Julian Oscillation and Eurasian snow also matter. Some studies suggest climate change makes ENSO extremes stronger. Treat claims with care.
India's climates and El Nino

Koppen's map for India: Am (Malabar), Aw (peninsula), BShw (semi-arid Deccan rain shadow), BWhw (Thar), Cwg (Gangetic plain), Dfc (Arunachal), and E (high Himalaya). Years like 2015 and 2023 (El Nino) brought below-normal rain; 2023 monsoon was about 94% of the long-period average. IMD now uses Mission Mausam (approved 2024) to improve forecasts.
How to write this

Likely questions "Describe the characteristics and distribution of the Mediterranean climate." (10 marks) "What is El Nino? How does it affect the Indian monsoon?" (10 marks) Structure: define; explain the normal Walker cell; show the break; list global effects; then India (monsoon, crops, prices, policy response). Prelims tip: Mediterranean = west coasts at 30-45 degrees; Peru's coast is where El Nino was first noticed; positive IOD aids the monsoon.
Ocean Relief, Temperature and Salinity
The oceans cover 71% of Earth

Fisheries, oil, minerals, trade routes and climate all depend on the ocean floor, its temperature and its salt. India has a coastline of about 11,098 km including islands (re-measured in 2025) and an Exclusive Economic Zone of about 2 million sq km.
The shape of the ocean floor
Most ocean floor is the abyssal plain, covered with deep mud called ooze . Sediment thins away from the coast.
Ridges, seamounts and trenches

Mid-ocean ridges are underwater mountain chains where plates diverge (Mid-Atlantic Ridge). Seamounts are submerged volcanoes; flat-topped ones are guyots . Trenches are mostly in the Pacific; the Mariana Trench, with Challenger Deep at about 11 km, is the deepest known point. Mid-ocean ridges plus deep trenches make the "Ring of Fire" in the Pacific.
Coral reefs

Corals need warm clear water of 20-30 C, sunlight and salinity near 35 ppt, so they grow in shallow tropical seas, mostly between 30 N and 30 S, away from muddy river mouths. Types: fringing (touching land), barrier (lagoon between; Great Barrier Reef, the largest) and atoll (ring around a lagoon; Lakshadweep). Coral bleaching occurs when warm water makes corals expel their algae. India's reefs: Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep.
Ocean temperature

Sea surface temperature falls from about 27 C near the equator to near freezing at the poles. It is highest slightly north of the equator because land in the north holds heat. Warm currents raise temperature, cold ones lower it. In the north, enclosed seas can be warmer (Red Sea) and Arctic seas colder. Temperature falls with depth to near 0 to 4 C.
Salinity

Salinity is grams of salt per kilogram of seawater, about 35 on average. It rises with evaporation and falls with rain, river inflow and melting ice. Highest in the tropics (20-30 degrees), lower at the equator (rain) and at the poles (melt).
Why salinity matters

Salinity and temperature set the density of water. Dense water sinks and drives the deep thermohaline circulation , the "ocean conveyor belt" that moves heat around the planet. Freshwater from melting ice can weaken this circulation: a concern for Atlantic currents.
Ocean warming and deep-sea mining

The oceans absorb over 90% of the excess heat of global warming. Marine heatwaves kill coral and fish. Meanwhile countries race for polymetallic nodules (nickel, cobalt, manganese) on the deep seabed. Supporters see critical minerals for batteries. Critics fear unknown damage to deep ecosystems. The International Seabed Authority (ISA) is still writing rules.
The Indian Ocean floor and resources

Features: the Chagos-Laccadive Ridge (Lakshadweep sits on it), the Ninety East Ridge , and the Andaman-Nicobar ridge. India holds an ISA licence for about 75,000 sq km in the Central Indian Ocean Basin for nodules. The Deep Ocean Mission (2021) includes the Samudrayaan manned submersible project.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the factors affecting the salinity of ocean water." (10 marks) "Why does the Bay of Bengal have lower salinity than the Arabian Sea?" (10 marks) Structure: list the zones of relief with an unusual feature; factors of temperature and salinity; end with resources and India's programmes. Prelims tip: average salinity is 35 ppt; the Dead Sea is the saltiest; trenches are mostly in the Pacific.
Currents, Tides and Ocean Resources
Moving water shapes trade and climate

Currents decide where deserts, fog and fisheries occur. Tides decide when ships can enter ports. The sea also supplies fish, oil, gas and minerals. These are core topics for GS I and for the blue economy theme in current affairs.
What drives currents

Currents are large streams of water. Drivers: prevailing winds , Coriolis force , differences in temperature and salinity (density), gravity and coastlines. Currents flow clockwise in the northern gyres and anticlockwise in the southern.
Warm and cold currents

Warm currents flow from low to high latitudes. Cold currents flow towards the equator, usually along west coasts. Where they meet, as off Newfoundland, fog forms and plankton thrives, making rich fisheries (Grand Banks, Japan, North Sea).
Effects of currents on climate

The North Atlantic Drift keeps north-west European ports like Bergen ice-free. Cold currents along west coasts cut rainfall and form coastal deserts : Atacama and Namib. The Humboldt current is linked to El Nino collapses in Peru's anchovy fishery.
Indian Ocean: currents that reverse

Unlike the Atlantic and Pacific, the northern Indian Ocean has seasonally reversing currents, driven by the monsoon. In summer, the South-West Monsoon Drift flows eastward. In winter, the North-East Monsoon Drift flows westward. South of 10 S the circulation is a steady anticlockwise gyre. Hence ancient sailors used the monsoon to cross.
Tides
Tides come from the Moon's and Sun's gravity and Earth's spin. Narrow, funnel-shaped bays raise the range: the Bay of Fundy (about 16 m) is the highest. Tide energy and port design use these data.
Ocean resources

Living: fish, seaweed. Mineral: salt, magnesium, nodules, sand. Energy: oil and gas (Mumbai High), tidal and wave power, gas hydrates . The Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, 1982) gives a 12 nautical mile territorial sea, a 200 nautical mile EEZ , and rights to the extended continental shelf.
Blue economy: growth or damage?

The ocean may be a new growth engine, but overfishing, plastic and bottom trawling threaten it. The Gulf Stream-linked AMOC may be slowing due to meltwater, which could shift weather in Europe and monsoon patterns. Science is still unsure about timing.
India's tides and blue economy

India has large tides in the Gulf of Khambhat and the Gulf of Kutch (up to about 11 m at Kandla); both are tidal power sites. The Hooghly sees a tidal bore. India is among the top fish producers, second only to China, with about 9% of world aquatic production (FAO, 2026). Sagarmala develops ports; the Deep Ocean Mission (2021) and a Blue Economy policy frame the push. Mumbai High remains the largest offshore oil field.
How to write this

Likely questions "Describe the ocean currents of the Indian Ocean and how they differ from those of the Atlantic." (10 marks) "How do ocean currents influence the climate of coastal areas?" (10 marks) Structure: causes; examples in a table; effects (rain, fog, fisheries); Indian Ocean reversal; end with policy. Prelims tip: cold currents on west coasts of continents at 15-30 degrees; spring tides occur at new and full moon; EEZ is 200 nm.
Soils and Natural Vegetation of the World
Soil and plants tie climate to people

Soil decides what farmers can grow. Vegetation decides what animals and people can live there. Together with climate they give every region its character. UPSC asks for distribution and reasons : why laterite in the tropics, why chernozem in the steppes.
Soil: how it forms

Pedogenesis depends on five factors: parent material , climate , relief , organisms and time . Climate is the most active. Warm, wet climates cause fast chemical weathering; cold or dry ones cause slow formation. Soil is a living system, 45% mineral, 25% water, 25% air and 5% organic matter, roughly.
The soil profile
A vertical cut through soil is a profile . The A horizon is the most fertile. Leaching washes nutrients down; eluviation and illuviation move clay and iron from upper layers to the B horizon.
Zonal soils of the world
Laterite (Latin later, brick) forms by laterisation : silica leaches, iron and aluminium remain. Hardens on exposure, so it is used for bricks, as in Kerala and Karnataka.
Natural vegetation: the biomes
Natural vegetation grows without human help. Temperature, moisture, soil and relief decide its type. With height, vegetation changes like it does with latitude: altitudinal zonation .
Tropical and Mediterranean forests

Equatorial rainforest : evergreen, layered, rich in species. Hardwoods like mahogany and ebony, hard to harvest. Monsoon forests shed leaves in the dry season: teak, sal. Savanna : tall grass and scattered trees. Mediterranean vegetation has small, waxy, drought-proof leaves: olives, citrus and vines. These regions are the world's citrus and wine orchards, called "orchards of the world".
Grasslands, taiga and tundra

Temperate grasslands are among the world's great wheat and cattle regions. Taiga is coniferous (pine, spruce, fir) with softwood for paper and matches. Tundra has mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs on permafrost; reindeer are central to the ecosystem.
Is soil a renewable resource?

Soil forms at a few centimetres per thousand years but erodes in decades if bare. Deforestation, over-grazing and chemical farming cause degradation and desertification. The UN Convention to Combat Desertification ( UNCCD , 1994) works on this. The debate: grow more food now, or protect the slow-forming soil base for the future? India's answer includes Soil Health Cards (2015) and watershed programmes.
India's soils and vegetation

India's main soil types: alluvial, black (regur), red, laterite, arid and forest soils. Black soil comes from Deccan basalt and suits cotton. Laterite is in the Western Ghats and east coast. Natural vegetation ranges from Western Ghats rainforest to Thar scrub and Himalayan alpine meadows (more in the Indian lessons). India lost some forest in the Himalaya and Northeast through jhum and mining, but the Forest Survey of India reports slow net gains in cover (as of ISFR 2023).
How to write this

Likely questions "Explain the process of laterisation and its effect on the soils of tropical regions." (10 marks) "Why are temperate grasslands called the granaries of the world?" (10 marks) Structure: climate first, then soil, then vegetation, then human use. Prelims tip: match grasslands to their continents (pampas = Argentina, veld = South Africa, downs = Australia); chernozems are black earths of the steppe.
Himalayas, Northern Plains and Peninsular Plateau
India's relief explains its climate, rivers, soils and wars

The Himalaya block cold winds and trap the monsoon. The plains feed 1.4 billion people. The plateau holds India's minerals. Almost every Indian geography answer starts with these three. Questions often ask for comparisons and reasons .
Six physiographic divisions
Physiography means the study of landforms. India's land area is about 3.28 million sq km. It spans 8 degrees 4 minutes N to 37 degrees 6 minutes N on the mainland.
The Himalaya: three parallel ranges
They are young fold mountains , about 2,400 km long, arched in a curve from the Indus gorge to the Dihang gorge. Each range has a different rock age and origin.
Himalayan divisions

Himadri holds Everest, Kanchenjunga (the highest peak in India, 8,586 m) and the glaciers. Himachal : Pir Panjal, Dhauladhar, Mussoorie, with hill stations and Kashmir valley. Shiwaliks : loose gravel and sandstone, with long valleys called duns (Dehradun) in Uttarakhand and duars in the east. By river (Sidney Burrard): Punjab (Indus to Sutlej), Kumaon (Sutlej to Kali), Nepal (Kali to Tista), Assam (Tista to Dihang).
The Northern Plains

Built by alluvium from the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra, about 7 lakh sq km. Divisions: Punjab-Haryana plain, Ganga plain, Brahmaputra plain. The plain slopes gently, and rivers form meanders , braided channels , and levees . Frequent floods go with high fertility.
The Peninsular Plateau

This is the oldest and most stable block, a part of Gondwanaland . The Narmada-Tapi flow in rift valleys, westwards. The Chotanagpur plateau is the mineral heartland. The Western Ghats are a block mountain edge, and rains to the west are heavy.
Gaps, passes and shape

Western Ghats gaps: Thal (Mumbai-Nashik), Bhor (Mumbai-Pune), Pal (Kerala-Tamil Nadu). Himalayan passes: Shipki La, Nathu La, Zoji La, Banihal, Rohtang, Jelep La. Mountain passes matter for trade and for military moves along the northern border.
Developing a fragile mountain

Himalayan roads, tunnels and hydropower bring jobs and security. Yet Joshimath sank in 2023, and the Uttarkashi Silkyara tunnel collapse (November 2023) and the 2013 Kedarnath and 2021 Chamoli floods show the risk. The Char Dham road debate pitted defence needs against ecology; the Supreme Court allowed a wider road in 2021 for the border.
Why the plains matter, and why the Himalaya shield

The Himalaya turn the monsoon back, so the Gangetic plains get rain, and they shield India from cold Central Asian winds. Glaciers feed the perennial rivers. The plains produce a large share of wheat and rice, and have about 40% of India's people. The Western Ghats are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012) and a biodiversity hotspot. The Himalaya are a hotspot too.
How to write this

Likely questions "Describe the physiographic divisions of India and their significance." (15 marks) "Himalayan range is vast and complex. Discuss how each range differs." (10 marks) Structure: list divisions; a short paragraph with key features and a number each; one line on economic or climatic significance; a current example. Prelims tip: Kanchenjunga is India's highest peak; Anamudi is the highest peak south of the Himalaya; Narmada flows west through a rift valley.
Coasts, Islands and Drainage Systems
Rivers, ports and islands

Rivers carry 1.4 billion people's water. Coasts carry 95% of India's trade by volume. Islands give India a strategic reach in the Indian Ocean. Questions mix physical facts (west-flowing rivers) with policy (rivers, ports, islands).
Western and eastern coasts

The east coast has big deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. The west coast has estuaries (Narmada, Tapi) because rivers cut straight, short courses to the sea. India's mainland coastline is about 6,100 km; with islands it is about 7,516 km (older figure). A re-measurement released in 2025 raised it to about 11,098 km, without any new land: modern mapping simply traces the coast in finer detail.
Lagoons, lakes and backwaters

Chilika (Odisha) is the largest coastal lagoon in India and the largest brackish lagoon in Asia, a Ramsar site. Pulicat sits on the Andhra-Tamil Nadu border. Kerala's kayals (Vembanad, Ashtamudi) are tourist backwaters. Sand bars separate them from the sea.
The islands

Lakshadweep: 32 sq km, separated from the Maldives by the Eight Degree channel and Minicoy by the Nine Degree channel. Andaman and Nicobar: about 570 islands, divided by the Ten Degree Channel . Narcondam is dormant; Barren Island is active. Islands matter as a strategic outpost near the Malacca Strait.
Two river systems
Antecedent means the river kept its course as the Himalaya rose. Peninsular rivers follow the slope.
The three big Himalayan rivers

Indus : from near Mansarovar, enters India in Ladakh, joined by the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. Ganga : Bhagirathi from Gangotri meets the Alaknanda at Devprayag. Tributaries: Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi, Son. Brahmaputra : from Tibet (Tsangpo), enters India as the Dihang, and flows through Assam.
Peninsular rivers and patterns
Godavari is the longest (about 1,465 km), called Dakshin Ganga. Krishna and Kaveri are vital for farming. The Narmada and Tapi flow west in rift valleys.
River management and cooperation

Brahmaputra dams in Tibet (China's Medog project, approved in December 2024) worry India about flows. The Indus Waters Treaty (1960) was held in abeyance by India in April 2025 after the Pahalgam attack. Within India, states fight over the Kaveri, Krishna and Godavari. Experts argue for basin-level planning.
Ganga and its cleaning

Ganga basin is about 26% of India's land and supports about 40% of its people. Namami Gange , started in 2014 under NMCG, built sewage plants. Ganga was declared the national river in 2008. The Ganga river dolphin is the national aquatic animal. The east coast's deltas are cyclone-prone. The west coast's estuaries (Narmada, Tapi) hold major ports like Surat and Hazira.
How to write this

Likely questions "Compare the east-flowing and west-flowing peninsular rivers." (10 marks) "Explain the strategic importance of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands." (10 marks) Structure: table-style comparison; reasons for the difference (gradient, rift valley); then a current issue (water sharing, ports). Prelims tip: know the channels (Eight, Nine, Ten Degree), Indira Point, Chilika, the Kaveri as a perennial-ish river with two monsoons, and that Godavari is the longest peninsular river.
The Indian Monsoon
Monsoon is India's real finance minister

Monsoon gives about 75% of annual rainfall, and farming employs a big share of workers. A weak monsoon raises food prices and cuts rural income. It features in GS I (climate), GS III (agriculture) and even Essay papers.
What is the monsoon?

The word comes from the Arabic mausim , meaning season. It is a seasonal reversal of winds: south-west in summer, north-east in winter. India's monsoon is the strongest because of the big landmass of Asia, the Tibetan plateau and the Indian Ocean.
Classical and modern explanations

Classical (Halley, 1686) : land heats faster than sea, giving a bigger sea breeze. Modern theory (Flohn, 1950s) ties it to the shift of the ITCZ: when the Sun moves north, the trough moves over the Ganga plain, and the south-east trades cross the equator, turning right to become south-west monsoon.
The onset and the two branches
The Arabian Sea branch is stronger and hits the Western Ghats first. The Bay of Bengal branch brings rain to the north-east and the Ganga plains. Onset is sudden: the burst .
Dates of the monsoon

Dates are normal values set by IMD; the onset over Kerala has varied from late May to early June in recent years. Withdrawal takes about a month, and October heat is the retreating monsoon with clear skies.
Spatial pattern

India's average rainfall is about 117 cm. Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in Meghalaya get over 1,100 cm; Jaisalmer gets under 10 cm. The Rain shadow east of the Western Ghats gets little. The north-east monsoon (October to December) is the main rain for Tamil Nadu. Rain comes in spells . Break monsoon is a gap of days when the trough shifts to the Himalaya foothills.
What disturbs it

El Nino (usually weakens), IOD (positive helps), Eurasian snow , MJO (a 30-60 day pulse) and western disturbances are key. IMD gives Long Period Average forecasts: normal is 96 to 104% of LPA (87 cm for 1971-2020 base). 2023: about 94% of LPA (El Nino); 2024: about 108%, above normal.
Is the monsoon changing?

Studies suggest fewer rainy days but more extreme downpours: floods in Kerala (2018), Chennai (2015), Himachal (2023). Some see a long-term weakening from aerosols; others see recovery with warming. For answers, say that the mean may be steady but variability is rising, which hits dryland farmers hardest.
Monsoon and the economy

A good monsoon lifts kharif crops (rice, pulses, cotton), reservoirs, hydropower and rural demand. A bad one raises food inflation, leading to export curbs on rice or sugar (as in 2023). IMD issues forecasts in April and updates in May and June. Mission Mausam aims at better models. Crop insurance (PMFBY) and contingency plans cushion shocks.
How to write this

Likely questions "Explain the mechanism of the south-west monsoon. Why is its onset sudden?" (15 marks) "What are the causes of break in the monsoon?" (10 marks) Structure: mechanism (ITCZ, jets, Tibet) with a diagram; onset and withdrawal dates; regional pattern; risks; economy. Prelims tip: know the normal onset date, the tropical easterly jet, the 87 cm LPA, and the retreating monsoon in October.
Soils, Forests and Natural Vegetation of India
Soil and forest are slow capital

Soil takes centuries to form; forests take decades. They support farms, water and wildlife, and are central to India's climate promise. Expect UPSC to link them to land degradation , mangroves and forest law.
Eight Indian soil types
ICAR groups India's soils into eight: alluvial, black, red, laterite, arid, saline, peaty and forest soils. Alluvial soil is the largest and most fertile, with Khadar new and Bhangar old.
Black and red soils

Black soil (regur) forms from Deccan basalt. It is rich in clay, holds moisture, cracks in summer (so it "self-ploughs") and is high in lime, iron and magnesium, low in nitrogen and humus. It is the home of cotton. Red soil gets its colour from iron in crystalline rock. It is porous and poor in humus, nitrogen and lime. It turns yellow when hydrated. It occurs in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.
Other soils

Laterite : leached by heavy rain; needs manure; suits tree crops. Arid : sandy, salty, low organic matter; Rajasthan. Saline and alkaline (reh, kallar, usar): too much salt, from poor irrigation. Peaty : Kerala (kari), rich in organic matter. Forest : hill soils, acidic in higher areas.
Soil erosion and conservation

Forms: sheet, rill and gully (the Chambal ravines). Causes: deforestation, over-grazing, heavy rain and bad ploughing. Remedies: contour ploughing , terracing , strip cropping, shelter belts , check dams and afforestation. The Central Soil Conservation Board was set up in 1953.
Forest types
Classification follows Champion and Seth (1968) : 16 major types. Rainfall is the main control, with temperature and altitude. Himalayan forests change with height in belts.
Forest cover today

As of ISFR 2023 , forest cover is about 21.76% of India's area; forest and tree cover together make about 25.2% (ISFR 2023). The target in the National Forest Policy 1988 is 33% of area (two thirds in hills). Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest cover in area; Mizoram the highest share. Very dense forest is only a small slice, so quality matters more than the headline.
Mangroves and tidal forests
Mangroves have stilt and breathing roots, protect coasts from storm surge and nurse fish. India has about 4,990 sq km (ISFR 2023); West Bengal leads.
Development versus forests

The Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023 exempts some categories (like linear projects near borders and security land) from clearance. Supporters see faster infrastructure; critics fear loss of undocumented forests. The Great Nicobar project raises a similar clash. Tribal rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 add a third view.
Policies and programmes

Green India Mission , CAMPA (compensatory afforestation funds), the Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam plantation drive (2024) and a pledge at COP26 for a 2.5-3 billion tonne carbon sink by 2030. Soil: Soil Health Card (2015) and Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana promote organic farming.
How to write this

Likely questions "Why is black soil considered the best for cotton? Where is it found?" (10 marks) "Discuss the status of mangroves in India and why they matter." (10 marks) Structure: classify; give origin of each soil with a crop; forest types by rainfall; recent data; law and policy. Prelims tip: memorise ISFR headline numbers, the biggest mangrove area (Sundarbans), and who proposed forest types (Champion and Seth).
Water Resources and River Interlinking
India has 18% of people and 4% of water

Water is the sharpest long-term constraint on India's growth. Rainfall is seasonal, rivers are unevenly spread, and groundwater is falling. UPSC links this to agriculture , federalism (water is a state subject) and interlinking .
How much water is there?

BCM means billion cubic metres. Only a fraction can be stored or used. India's per capita availability has fallen from about 5,000 cubic m in 1951 to about 1,500 in 2021, so India is officially water-stressed .
Where it goes

Irrigation dominates use. Groundwater supplies about 60% of irrigation and 85% of rural drinking water. India is the world's largest extractor of groundwater, which is why states like Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan have many over-exploited blocks.
Dams and multipurpose projects

Big dams: Bhakra (Sutlej), Hirakud (Mahanadi), Tehri (Bhagirathi, tallest in India), Sardar Sarovar (Narmada). Dams give irrigation, power, flood control and water supply, but cause displacement, siltation and loss of habitat. Jawaharlal Nehru called dams the temples of modern India.
Interlinking: the idea

Surplus river basins (Brahmaputra, Ganga, Mahanadi) could pass water to deficit ones (Cauvery, Pennar, western Rajasthan). The National Perspective Plan (1980) proposed 30 links: 16 peninsular and 14 Himalayan. The NWDA (1982) studies them. The Supreme Court in 2012 directed the Centre to act.
The Ken-Betwa link

The first project under the national plan was approved in 2021 and its foundation stone laid in December 2024. It moves water from the Ken to the Betwa for drought-hit Bundelkhand across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh. It will submerge part of the Panna Tiger Reserve, a main criticism.
Is interlinking wise?

For: drought and flood relief, irrigation, navigation. Against: huge cost, displacement, damaged ecosystems, effects on the Ganga delta and monsoon, and state disputes over whether any state has a "surplus". Critics favour cheaper local options: rainwater harvesting , watershed work, drip irrigation, and fixing leaky canals.
Interstate disputes and law

Water is a State subject (Entry 17, State List), but Article 262 lets Parliament settle interstate river disputes through the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 . Tribunals have sat for Cauvery (award 2007, modified by the Supreme Court in 2018), Krishna and Godavari. Disputes drag on for decades.
Programmes

Jal Shakti Ministry (2019); Jal Jeevan Mission (2019): tap water to every rural home; Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019): community groundwater management in stressed areas; PMKSY (2015): "more crop per drop"; Amrit Sarovar (2022): 75 ponds per district; and the Jal Shakti Abhiyan catch-the-rain campaign.
How to write this

Likely questions "Examine the feasibility of river interlinking in India." (15 marks) "How can India address groundwater depletion?" (10 marks) Structure: status; opportunity; concerns (ecology, federal, costs); alternatives; give Ken-Betwa as a current test. Prelims tip: NWDA, the 30 links, Article 262, and the Ken-Betwa states are repeat hits.
Agriculture: Cropping Patterns and Irrigation
Farming employs nearly half of India

Agriculture and allied sectors employ about 46% of workers but give about 18% of GVA (as of recent years). So farm policy is a big political economy issue. UPSC mixes geography (where, why) with policy (MSP, irrigation, diversification).
Farming types and seasons
Types: subsistence , commercial , plantation (tea, coffee, rubber), shifting (jhum in the Northeast), dry farming in under 75 cm rain regions, and intensive farming in the plains.
Main crops and where they grow

Crops follow rainfall, temperature and soil. Rice is the staple of the east and south. Wheat dominates the north-west. Millets (shree anna) grow in dry regions; 2023 was the International Year of Millets.
Cash and plantation crops

Cotton and jute are fibres; jute grows in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta of West Bengal. Sugarcane is needed for sugar mills. Tea (Assam), coffee (Karnataka, Kodagu) and rubber (Kerala) are plantations. India is the second largest producer of tea and of rice, wheat and sugar too, as of recent data.
Irrigation

Net irrigated area is about 55% of net sown area. Wells and tubewells lead because they are cheap and farmer-controlled, but they deplete the groundwater table. Tanks are common where rock is hard. Drip and sprinkler systems save water.
The Green Revolution

From the mid-1960s, HYV seeds (Norman Borlaug; M.S. Swaminathan in India), fertiliser, irrigation and credit raised wheat and then rice output in Punjab, Haryana and western UP. India became self-sufficient in food grains. Limits: regional and crop bias, soil degradation, falling water tables.
Is the Punjab model sustainable?

Punjab and Haryana grow rice in a dry region because MSP and procurement favour it. Groundwater falls about a metre a year in some blocks, and stubble burning pollutes Delhi. Experts urge crop diversification to pulses, maize and oilseeds, direct-seeded rice and price signals. Others warn farmers will not shift without assured purchase.
Policy at a glance

MSP is declared by the Centre on CACP advice for 22 crops plus FRP for sugarcane. PM-KISAN (2019) gives cash. PMFBY (2016) is crop insurance. e-NAM links mandis. The three farm laws were repealed in 2021 after farmer protests. The government's target is to double farmer income, widely seen as missed.
New frontiers

Horticulture output now exceeds food grains. Operation Flood (1970) made India the largest milk producer. The Northeast and Odisha show jhum being replaced slowly. Natural farming mission launched in 2024 and drone use (Namo Drone Didi) are fresh themes. The Kharif crops depend on monsoon; Rabi on stored moisture and irrigation.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the changing cropping pattern in India and its causes." (10 marks) "Examine the importance of irrigation in Indian agriculture." (10 marks) Structure: trend in numbers; physical factors; policy factors (MSP, irrigation); impact (water, soil); way forward. Prelims tip: match crops to seasons and states; rice is kharif; wheat is rabi; MSP is set on CACP advice.
Minerals and Energy Resources
Minerals build, energy drives

India's rise needs steel, aluminium, power and fuel. The geography question is where the resources are and why industry sits near them. The new question is critical minerals and the move to clean energy.
Mineral belts of India

Most metallic minerals lie in the old rocks of the peninsula . The Himalayan region has few. The Gangetic plains have almost none, apart from building materials. Mining is regulated by the MMDR Act, 1957 , amended in 2015, 2021 and 2023.
Key minerals at a glance

Iron ore types: hematite (best, about 60-70% iron) and magnetite (highest iron content). Famous mines: Bailadila (Chhattisgarh), Kudremukh (Karnataka), Noamundi (Jharkhand). India has large reserves of iron ore, mica and bauxite but is short of coking coal and copper.
Coal

Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Odisha hold the biggest reserves. Jharia is the main coking coal field; Raniganj (West Bengal) is the oldest. India produced over one billion tonnes of coal in 2024-25 (as of 2025), yet still imports coking coal.
Petroleum and gas

First oil: Digboi in Assam (1889). Main fields: Mumbai High (offshore), Assam, Gujarat (Ankleshwar, Cambay) and the Krishna-Godavari basin. India imports about 85% of its crude oil (as of recent data). Strategic reserves are at Vishakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.
Power sources
Hydro projects: Bhakra, Tehri, Koyna. Nuclear: India uses uranium and plans a three-stage programme to use its large thorium reserves in Kerala sands. Kudankulam in Tamil Nadu has Russian reactors.
Renewables and green hydrogen

The Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan is among the world's largest. Wind is big in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat. India's target: 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070 . The International Solar Alliance (2015) is headquartered in Gurugram. The National Green Hydrogen Mission began in 2023. Non-fossil sources reached about half of installed capacity in 2025.
Coal now, clean later?

Coal supplies most of India's electricity and mines support lakhs of jobs in Jharkhand and Odisha. A fast shutdown would hurt them. But coal causes air pollution and emissions. The debate centres on a just transition : retrain workers, keep coal for baseload, and add storage plus renewables, while demand grows.
Critical minerals

Lithium, cobalt and rare earths are needed for batteries and magnets. India found lithium at Reasi in J&K (2023) and set up the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025). Overseas, KABIL buys assets in Argentina and Australia. China's control of processing worries India.
How to write this

Likely questions "Describe the distribution of iron ore in India and its role in steel plant location." (10 marks) "Is India's energy transition feasible without coal?" (15 marks) Structure: distribution; link to industries; problems (imports, environment); energy mix; policy such as the 2030 and 2070 goals. Prelims tip: Gondwana coal is 98%; Digboi is the first oil field; Jharia is the coking coal hub.
Industrial Location and Industrial Regions
Where factories go

Factories choose places to cut cost and raise sales. The answer shapes cities, rivers, ports and regional inequality. For UPSC, you must explain why an industry is located where it is , and link it to current manufacturing policy.
Weber's location theory

Alfred Weber (1909) argued firms pick the point with the least transport cost , then adjust for labour and agglomeration. If the raw material loses weight in processing (ore to iron), the factory goes near the raw material. If it gains weight or is perishable, it goes to the market.
Factors of location in India

Raw material, power, water, labour, capital, market, transport, government policy and history all matter. Weight-losing industries such as iron and steel and sugar go near sources. Footloose industries such as IT and electronics can go anywhere, so skilled labour and urban facilities decide.
Iron and steel

Steel plants sit in the Chotanagpur belt because iron ore, coking coal, limestone and manganese are close. After 1990 the private sector and coastal sites (Visakhapatnam, Gujarat Hazira) rose. India is the second largest crude steel producer, after China (as of recent data).
Cotton, sugar and other industries

Cotton textiles : early mills in Mumbai (1854) and Ahmedabad thanks to port, capital and cotton; now spread widely, with spinning in the south. Sugar : shifted from UP to Maharashtra because cane has higher sucrose in the tropical climate and cooperatives helped. Cement : near limestone. Aluminium : near cheap power and bauxite.
Industrial regions
Other regions: Chotanagpur , Delhi-Gurugram-Meerut, and Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram. Most clusters grew around ports and old mineral belts. Eastern India has resources but lags in new industry.
Policy and corridors

Industrial Policy Resolution 1956 gave the public sector a dominant role; 1991 liberalised licensing. Make in India (2014) and PLI schemes (2020) aim to lift manufacturing to 25% of GDP. Industrial corridors (Delhi-Mumbai, Chennai-Bengaluru) and SEZs (Act 2005) cluster factories. PM GatiShakti (2021) coordinates transport links.
Spread industry or let clusters grow?

Clusters bring economies of scale, but regional inequality grows: four states (Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Karnataka) host a large share of factory output. Policy tools like tax holidays and corridors in backward areas are used. Critics point to land acquisition, displacement and pollution in such sites.
Current moves

Semiconductor fabs in Dholera (Gujarat) and Assam, mobile phone assembly in Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh, and defence corridors in UP and Tamil Nadu are the newest clusters. Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra lead in electronics and autos. MSMEs account for about a third of manufacturing output.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the factors influencing the location of iron and steel industry in India." (10 marks) "Account for the decline of Mumbai textile mills and the rise of Surat." (10 marks) Structure: theory first (Weber), then Indian factors, examples, regional pattern, policy. Prelims tip: TISCO is the oldest steel plant; Bhilai and Bokaro came with the USSR; Rourkela with Germany; Durgapur with the UK.
Transport and Communication
Roads and ports make markets

Transport links farms to cities and India to the world. High logistics costs cut competitiveness. In GS I you must explain patterns of networks ; in GS III you link them to growth and trade, so both views are needed.
Modes at a glance
India has the second largest road network in the world, over 60 lakh km, of which national highways are about 1.4 lakh km. Roads carry the largest share, which raises costs and emissions.
Roads and expressways

The National Highways Authority of India was set up in 1988. Projects: the Golden Quadrilateral, the North-South and East-West corridors (7,300 km) and Bharatmala (2017). Expressways such as Delhi-Mumbai are underway. PMGSY (2000) connects villages.
Railways

The first train ran from Bombay to Thane in 1853 (34 km). Indian Railways is run by the state and divided into 17 zones. The network is among the world's largest by route length (about 68,000 km). Dedicated Freight Corridors (Eastern: Ludhiana to Sonnagar; Western: Dadri to JNPT) free up passenger lines. Vande Bharat trains and the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project are the newest steps.
Ports and shipping

Around 95% of trade by volume and about 70% by value moves by sea. Sagarmala (2015) aims at port-led growth. A new deep-water Vadhavan port in Maharashtra was approved in 2024, and Vizhinjam in Kerala is the first deep-water transhipment port (opened in 2025).
Waterways and air

NW-1 on the Ganga (Haldia to Prayagraj, 1,620 km), NW-2 on the Brahmaputra (Dhubri to Sadiya) and NW-3 on the West Coast canal are the first three. The 2016 Act declared 111 national waterways. Airways: UDAN (2016) links small cities; the airport count more than doubled in a decade (as of 2024).
Communication

India has the second largest telecom subscriber base. 5G launched in October 2022. Digital India (2015), BharatNet for villages, and UPI now account for the largest volume of real-time payments in the world. Postal network is the largest by number of outlets. ISRO satellites (INSAT, GSAT) support all of this.
Roads, rail or water?

Logistics cost in India is about 8% of GDP by the official NCAER estimate (2024), down from older estimates of 13-14% (figures vary by method). Experts urge a shift from roads to rail and waterways. The National Logistics Policy (2022) and PM GatiShakti seek this. Critics say inland waterways have too little traffic to justify costs.
Connectivity and geopolitics

Chabahar port (Iran) offers a route to Afghanistan and Central Asia, avoiding Pakistan. The International North-South Transport Corridor links India, Iran and Russia. The India-Middle East-Europe Corridor ( IMEC , announced at G20, 2023) is another plan. Border roads and tunnels in the Himalaya (Atal Tunnel, 2020) serve security as well as trade.
How to write this

Likely questions "Examine the role of inland waterways in India's transport system." (10 marks) "How do ports and logistics determine export competitiveness?" (15 marks) Structure: mode share; problems; schemes; modal shift; link to geopolitics. Prelims tip: NW-1 is on the Ganga; GQ links the four metros; Sagarmala is for ports; UDAN is for regional air connectivity.
Population, Migration and Urbanisation
People are the resource and the problem

India became the world's most populous country in 2023 (UN estimate). Numbers decide seats , grants , schemes and the economy. Age profile creates the demographic dividend . UPSC asks about trends, regional contrasts, migration and cities.
Key figures

Population growth has slowed. The fertility rate is now below the replacement level of 2.1. The census due in 2021 was delayed by COVID-19; the next census was announced for 2027 with caste enumeration (as of the 2025 notification).
Demographic transition

Stage 1 : high births, high deaths. Stage 2 : deaths fall first, population booms. Stage 3 : births fall. Stage 4 : low births, low deaths. Some add a fifth stage of ageing and decline (Japan). India's states are in different stages: Kerala and Tamil Nadu are late; Bihar and Uttar Pradesh are earlier.
Demographic dividend and ageing

A dividend arises when the working age (15-64) share is high. India's window runs to about 2040-50. It pays only if there are jobs, skills and health . Otherwise it is a "demographic burden". Southern states are ageing faster, with elderly share rising.
Migration

The 2011 Census counted about 45.6 crore migrants (37% of the population), mostly women moving for marriage. Men migrate for work. The 2020 lockdown exposed circular migrants' fragility; the One Nation One Ration Card and e-Shram portal followed.
Urbanisation

The urban share was 31% in 2011 and is estimated around mid-30s now. Cities: Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata (the three mega-cities of 2011), then Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad. A census town has 5,000 people, 75% non-farm male workers and density 400 per sq km. Problems: slums, traffic, floods, pollution, weak municipal finance.
Regional pattern of growth and density

The Gangetic plains, coasts and Kerala are densely settled; deserts, Himalaya and the Northeast are thin. Uttar Pradesh is the largest state by population; Sikkim is the smallest. Bihar has the highest density among states (1,106 per sq km in 2011); Arunachal Pradesh the lowest. Reasons: fertile alluvium, water, history of farming, and now job-centres. Low density in hill states reflects relief and climate.
Delimitation and population control

Seats in the Lok Sabha are frozen on 1971 numbers until the first census after 2026 (Articles 82 and 170). If seats follow today's population, northern states with higher growth gain and southern states lose share, though they did better at population control. The debate is about fairness: should success in family planning be penalised?
Schemes and planning

Smart Cities (2015), AMRUT (2015, urban water), Swachh Bharat (2014), PM Awas , and Mission Shakti for women. The National Population Policy 2000 set the goal of reaching replacement TFR; Mission Parivar Vikas targets high-fertility districts. Regional contrasts: Kerala sex ratio above 1,000; Haryana among the lowest.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the main features of India's demographic transition and the demographic dividend." (15 marks) "Examine the causes and consequences of rural-urban migration." (10 marks) Structure: data; theory; regional contrasts; opportunities and risks; schemes. Prelims tip: Census 2011 literacy is 74.04%, sex ratio 943; the replacement level TFR is 2.1.
Distribution of Key Natural Resources
Resources shape power

Oil built the Gulf's wealth and the world's wars. Cobalt and lithium will shape the next era. Where resources lie, who controls them, and how they are traded is a basic GS I theme, and it links to international relations.
Kinds of resources
Another split: biotic (forests, fish) and abiotic (minerals, water). Resources become reserves when they can be mined profitably. Technology and price change what counts as a resource.
Fossil fuels

Oil lies in a few basins: the Persian Gulf (about half of known reserves), the US, Russia and Canada's oil sands. Venezuela claims the largest proven reserves. OPEC (1960) has 12 members as of 2024 and OPEC+ includes Russia. Coal is widely spread and burned mostly for power and steel.
Metals

Iron ore lies in old shield areas, which is why Australia, Brazil, India and South Africa lead. Copper is concentrated along the Andes. Many figures change each year; check the latest USGS or industry data for exact ranks.
Critical minerals and the lithium triangle

Lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite and rare earths go into batteries, wind turbines and chips. The lithium triangle (Chile, Argentina, Bolivia) holds large brine reserves. The DR Congo supplies most cobalt, often with child labour. China processes most of the world's rare earths and battery materials, giving it leverage.
Water, forests and fisheries

Only about 2.5% of water is fresh, and most of that is in ice. Forests: Amazon , Congo basin , Siberian taiga, boreal Canada. Fisheries: Grand Banks, Peruvian anchovy, North Sea, East Asia. Overfishing is a global problem; the high seas have no single owner. UN High Seas treaty (BBNJ) was adopted in 2023.
Trade routes and chokepoints

Resources travel by sea through narrow straits: Hormuz (about a fifth of world oil), Malacca (between Indonesia and Malaysia, links the Indian and Pacific oceans), Bab-el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal . Attacks on shipping in the Red Sea since late 2023 pushed ships round the Cape of Good Hope. Pipelines such as Druzhba (Russia to Europe) matter for gas and oil on land.
Resource curse or blessing?

Many resource-rich states, such as Nigeria, Venezuela and DR Congo, suffer from corruption, conflict and a weak industry (the resource curse or "Dutch disease"). Others, like Norway, avoided it with a sovereign wealth fund and strong institutions. Resource nationalism (Indonesia banning raw nickel exports) is rising. The lesson: institutions decide outcomes.
India's resource position

India has coal, iron ore, bauxite and mica but imports about 85% of oil, most gas, and nearly all lithium and cobalt. It holds large thorium reserves. To fix this it uses strategic reserves , buys foreign assets via ONGC Videsh and KABIL, and joins the Minerals Security Partnership (2022). The Arctic and Antarctic (Himadri and Bharati stations) add a polar resource angle.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the global distribution of petroleum and its geopolitical implications." (15 marks) "Why are critical minerals central to the energy transition? What are India's vulnerabilities?" (15 marks) Structure: map the distribution; reasons (geology); trade patterns; politics; India's dependency and response. Prelims tip: Chile is the top copper miner; DR Congo has most cobalt; OPEC was founded in 1960 in Baghdad.
Factors in the Location of Industries Worldwide
Industry follows cost and opportunity

Why did steel go to the Ruhr and phones to Shenzhen? Why is the Rust Belt rusting? Location theory explains the map of world industry. In mains, answer with factors, a theory and a changing pattern , with Indian links.
Classic factors

Raw material (weight-losing industries stay near it), power (aluminium), market (bulky or perishable goods), labour (textiles), capital , transport , water , land , government policy (SEZs, tax breaks) and agglomeration , where firms cluster to share suppliers and workers. Industrial inertia means industries stay after the original reason has gone.
Weber and beyond

Weber (1909) gave the least-cost model. Hotelling (1929) added competition: sellers cluster to share the market. Losch looked at market areas. Vernon's product cycle (1966) suggested new products start in rich countries, then move to cheaper ones as they mature. Porter (1990) argued clusters create competitive advantage.
Major industrial regions

Traditional: Ruhr (Germany), Great Lakes (USA, steel and cars), Donbas (Ukraine), Midlands (UK), Kanto and Kansai (Japan). New: Pearl River Delta and Yangtze delta (China), Seoul, Taiwan, and Silicon Valley . Many older regions declined; some rebuilt themselves with services and technology.
Shifting centre of gravity
Reasons: cheaper labour, big markets, trade liberalisation, containerisation and global value chains. Brands design in one place and assemble in another.
Technology and footloose industries

Electronics, software and pharma depend on skills, research and airports more than on coal or ore. Their location depends on universities , venture capital and urban quality. 3D printing and AI may make production more local. Just-in-time supply (Toyota) shows how coordination matters as much as cost.
Case study: policy can create a location

China set up Special Economic Zones in 1980 (Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Shantou, Xiamen) under Deng Xiaoping. A fishing town, Shenzhen became a global electronics hub within decades. Cheap labour was not enough: ports, tax breaks, foreign capital and WTO entry (2001) all helped. India's SEZ Act of 2005 copied the idea, with mixed results due to land and tax problems.
Reshoring, tariffs and supply chain risk

COVID-19 and trade wars exposed risks of concentrating in one country. The US CHIPS Act (2022), Europe's Chips Act and tariff moves aim to bring production home or to friendly states ("friend-shoring"). Critics fear higher prices and fragmentation. China remains central to most supply chains, so full decoupling is hard.
Where India fits

India aims to gain from China plus one . Apple's contract makers have set up in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka; autos cluster in Chennai, Pune and Gurugram; pharma in Hyderabad. India's PLI schemes and semiconductor mission (2021) seek fabs. Problems: logistics costs, land, power quality, and labour law. See also the lesson on Indian industrial regions.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the factors responsible for the shifting of the industrial centre of gravity to East Asia." (15 marks) "Why have older industrial regions of the world declined? Give examples." (10 marks) Structure: factors; theory; shift timeline; two examples; India's opportunity and obstacles. Prelims tip: Ruhr = coal and steel; Silicon Valley = software and chips; Pearl River Delta = electronics.
Population Theories and Settlements
Numbers, food and the places we live

Will the world run out of food? Why do cities have the shape they do? These two questions give us population theories and settlement geography. For mains, know who said what and when, and link to India's ageing, migration and cities.
Malthus, 1798

Thomas Malthus , An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798): population grows geometrically, food arithmetically. Positive checks (famine, disease, war) and preventive checks (late marriage, restraint) keep numbers in line. Neo-Malthusians (Paul Ehrlich, The Population Bomb , 1968; the Club of Rome's Limits to Growth , 1972) added resource limits.
Critics: Boserup and Marx

Ester Boserup , The Conditions of Agricultural Growth (1965), reversed the logic: population pressure forces innovation and intensive farming. "Necessity is the mother of invention." Marx said poverty arises from capitalist social structure, not from numbers. Green Revolution and technology so far have supported Boserup more than Malthus.
Transition and optimum population

Demographic transition (Thompson 1929, Notestein 1945) links fertility fall to development. Optimum population (Edwin Cannan; Alfred Sauvy) is the number that gives the best living standard with available resources. Above it is overpopulation, below it underpopulation. It is hard to measure because technology and trade shift the optimum.
Rural settlements

Pattern depends on terrain, water, defence and culture. In India, compact villages dominate the plains; dispersed hamlets in the hills, Northeast and tribal areas; linear villages along roads and rivers in Kerala and the Ganga valley.
Urban structure models

Burgess (1925) : concentric zones around the CBD (Chicago). Hoyt (1939) : wedges along transport lines. Harris and Ullman (1945) : several nuclei. Indian cities show mixtures with colonial cores and slum pockets.
Central place theory

Walter Christaller (1933) said settlements form a hierarchy: many villages, fewer towns, one city. Each serves a market area. Higher-order goods need a larger threshold and range. Hexagons are the most efficient shape.
City size and hierarchy

Primate city (Mark Jefferson, 1939): a city far bigger than the next, such as Bangkok or Paris. Rank-size rule (Zipf): the nth city is 1/n of the biggest. Conurbation (Patrick Geddes, 1915): merged towns, like Greater Manchester. Megacity : above 10 million people.
Is overpopulation the problem?

Neo-Malthusians point to climate and water limits. Others say consumption , not numbers, drives the pressure, since the richest countries use far more resources per head. Many countries now face falling fertility and ageing (Japan, China, South Korea). A balanced view: both numbers and consumption matter, and outcomes depend on policy.
India: settlements and slums

Indian cities are marked by primate-like growth (Mumbai, Delhi) and by slums; Dharavi in Mumbai is a well-known case. Smart Cities and AMRUT target infrastructure, and the Census defines towns. Many Indian villages are clustered along caste lines; rural-urban fringes see "peri-urban" sprawl.
How to write this

Likely questions "Critically examine Malthusian theory in the Indian context." (10 marks) "Discuss the urban land-use models and their relevance to Indian cities." (15 marks) Structure: theory, year, author; strengths; criticism; Indian evidence (Green Revolution, ageing, migration). Prelims tip: Malthus 1798; Boserup 1965; Burgess 1925 concentric; Christaller 1933 central place.
Salient Features of World Physical Geography
A mental map saves marks

Prelims and mains both reward a clear mental map of the world: where mountains, rivers, seas and straits lie. This lesson is a revision capsule. Learn it with an atlas open and quiz yourself on locations.
Continents and oceans
Mountain systems
Most great ranges follow plate boundaries. The Pacific "Ring of Fire" circles the Pacific with young fold mountains and volcanoes (Andes, Rockies, Japan).
Rivers

The Nile and the Amazon are often argued as the longest; recent studies suggest the Amazon could be as long as or longer. For exams, the safe answer is the Nile . Rivers draining to enclosed seas include the Volga (Caspian) and the Amu and Syr Darya (Aral).
Lakes and deserts

The Great Lakes of North America hold a large share of surface fresh water; Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake by area. Lake Baikal is the deepest and holds about 20% of the world's liquid fresh water. Deserts: Sahara, Arabian, Gobi, Atacama (driest), Kalahari, Thar. Antarctica is the largest by area.
Straits, canals and chokepoints

Suez Canal (opened 1869) links the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. Panama Canal (1914) links the Atlantic and Pacific. Straits: Gibraltar, Bosphorus, Hormuz, Malacca, Bab-el-Mandeb, Bering. These control the flow of oil, grain and goods, and are central to international relations.
Lines on the globe

Latitude lines are parallel; longitudes meet at the poles. The Prime Meridian runs through Greenwich; the International Date Line follows 180 degrees. The Sun is overhead between the Tropics. Days become polar near the circles.
Facts that change

Everest was officially re-measured at 8,848.86 m by China and Nepal in 2020. The Aral Sea has shrunk drastically since 1960 because of cotton irrigation. Arctic sea ice and glaciers are in retreat. Treat many "record" numbers as approximate and say "about" or "as of" in answers.
India's place on the world map

The mainland lies between 8 and 37 degrees N, so the Tropic of Cancer splits it nearly in half. India is the seventh largest country by area and has land borders with six countries (seven if Afghanistan is counted through PoK). Himalaya and the Indian Ocean frame it. The Indian Ocean linking Africa, the Gulf and East Asia explains India's sea power role.
How to write this

Likely questions "Mention the major straits and canals of the world and explain their strategic importance." (10 marks) "Locate on a map and explain the importance of the Malacca Strait." (10 marks) Structure: locate; give a number; add one strategic or economic point; link to India. Prelims tip: sketch a rough world map and drill locations of seas, straits, deserts and mountain ranges.
Changes in Critical Geographical Features
Maps are being redrawn

Glaciers retreat, lakes dry up, coasts move and species shift. GS I asks you to explain causes and effects of such changes, from sea-level rise to the death of the Aral Sea. Always separate natural cycles from human-driven change.
What has changed

Global average temperature is about 1.1 to 1.2 C above the 1850-1900 level (IPCC AR6, 2021). 2024 was the warmest year on record and the first calendar year above 1.5 C (WMO, as of 2025). Greenhouse gases from fossil fuels, cement and land-use change are the main cause. Ice, oceans and living things all respond.
Ice caps and glaciers
Arctic summer sea ice is shrinking by about 12% a decade. Greenland and Antarctica lose ice, and the Thwaites glacier is a worry. Melting sea ice does not raise sea level directly; land ice does.
Sea level rise

Sea level has risen about 20 cm since 1900 and the rate is now about 4 mm a year (IPCC AR6, WMO). The coasts of deltas, small islands and big port cities (Mumbai, Kolkata, Dhaka, Jakarta) are most at risk.
Water bodies: lakes and seas
Causes are mostly human: diversion for irrigation, groundwater pumping and urban growth, plus drought. Effects: dust storms, loss of fisheries, health hazards and migration.
Flora and fauna
