Species move to cooler places, up hills and towards the poles. Coral reefs bleach when seas get hotter; the world is in a fourth global bleaching event (2023 onward, NOAA). Forests face fires and pests. Habitat loss, over-exploitation, invasive species and pollution add pressure: the IPBES report of 2019 warned that about a million species face extinction.
Permafrost, glaciers and hazards

Thawing permafrost releases methane and CO2 and damages roads and pipelines in Siberia and Alaska. Mountain glaciers feed glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) . Himalayan glaciers are retreating on average, and the 2023 South Lhonak lake burst in Sikkim damaged the Teesta III dam.
Tipping points: are we past them?

Scientists warn of tipping points : collapse of the West Antarctic ice sheet, Amazon dieback, Atlantic circulation slowdown, coral die-off. Timing is uncertain, but the risk rises with each tenth of a degree. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims at under 2 C. Critics doubt the pledges are enough; developing countries ask for climate finance and equity.
India's exposed features

Sundarbans are losing land (Ghoramara island has lost much area). The Himalayan glaciers (Gangotri retreat), the Western Ghats' shifting rainfall, and coastal Gujarat and Odisha face salt intrusion. Marine heatwaves threaten the Gulf of Mannar. India's National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008) has eight missions, and its net-zero target is 2070.
How to write this

Likely questions "How are melting glaciers and rising seas changing the geography of coasts? Illustrate with Indian examples." (15 marks) "Discuss the causes and consequences of the shrinking of the Aral Sea." (10 marks) Structure: cause (human and natural); evidence (data); effect on land, water, life and people; adaptation and mitigation. Prelims tip: ice-albedo feedback; melting sea ice does not raise sea level; GLOF; Ramsar sites are wetlands.
Disaster Types and India's Vulnerability
Nature gives hazards; people make disasters

India sits on active plates, borders a warming ocean and has a monsoon climate. Millions of poor and unprepared people live in exposed places. UPSC treats disasters as geography (causes) and as governance (response). This lesson covers the first part.
Hazard, risk and vulnerability

A hazard is a dangerous event. A disaster happens when a hazard hits a vulnerable community. The Disaster Management Act, 2005 defines a disaster as a catastrophe, mishap, calamity or grave occurrence that causes loss of life, property or damage to the environment beyond the community's capacity to cope.
Classification

Another split is by speed: rapid onset (earthquake, flash flood) and slow onset (drought, desertification). Disasters can cascade: a quake triggers a landslide, which blocks a river and floods a valley.
India's vulnerability: the numbers
These figures come from NDMA and similar sources; they change with updated maps. Most districts face at least one major hazard. Heat waves and lightning are now recognised as major killers.
Why India is so exposed

Geography : young Himalaya, a long coast, river basins in flood plains. Climate : monsoon variability, and warming seas. Society : dense population, poor housing, weak enforcement of building codes, encroachment on floodplains, and deforestation. Poverty is the biggest vulnerability, as poor people live in kutcha houses on risky land.
Major disasters to remember

Bhopal gas leak (1984), Odisha super cyclone (1999), Bhuj quake (2001), Indian Ocean tsunami (2004), Mumbai floods (2005), Uttarakhand floods (2013), Chennai floods (2015), Kerala floods (2018), Chamoli (2021), Wayanad landslides (July 2024, over 200 deaths), Himachal and Sikkim floods (2023).
Why each hazard strikes

Floods : heavy monsoon rain, silt-choked rivers (Kosi, the "sorrow of Bihar"), poor drainage, encroachment. Cyclones : warm Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea, shallow coastal shelf. Drought : monsoon failure, rain-shadow areas (Marathwada, Rayalaseema, Bundelkhand). Landslides : steep young slopes, heavy rain, road cutting and tunnelling. Heat waves : dry north-west winds and clear skies in April-June. Cloudbursts : rain above 10 cm in an hour over a small area in the hills.
Are disasters really "natural"?

Scholars argue that disasters are social : the same quake kills thousands in a poor country and few in a rich one. Kerala 2018 and Chennai 2015 followed unplanned building on wetlands and bad dam management. Others stress that climate change is increasing the hazards themselves. Both views matter: reduce exposure and vulnerability, and cut emissions.
Changing risk profile

Cities are the new frontier: urban floods in Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Delhi. Heat waves (2024 saw record temperatures in north India) and lightning kill many each year. Himalayan states face glacial floods and landslides. India has the Vulnerability Atlas (BMTPC) for housing and a national flood and landslide mapping effort.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the vulnerability profile of India to natural hazards." (15 marks) "Why are urban floods increasing in India? Suggest measures." (10 marks) Structure: define; classify; numbers; causes (natural plus human); recent cases; link to the framework in the next lesson. Prelims tip: DM Act 2005; Sendai Framework (2015-2030); Bhopal 1984 is the worst industrial disaster; Kerala floods 2018.
Disaster Management Framework in India
Moving from relief to resilience

Until 1999 India saw disasters as the job of the relief commissioner and Agriculture Ministry. The Odisha super cyclone (1999) and Bhuj quake (2001) changed that. Today law, funds and forces exist; the debate is about preparedness, federalism and local capacity.
The disaster management cycle
Mitigation (structural: embankments, codes; non-structural: zoning, laws), preparedness (warning, drills), response (search and rescue, relief), and recovery (rehabilitation, "build back better").
How the system evolved

1999 : High Powered Committee under J.C. Pant. 2001 : Gujarat quake, a national committee, and 10th Finance Commission. 2005 : the Disaster Management Act . 2006 : the NDRF. 2009 : National Policy on Disaster Management. 2016 : first National Disaster Management Plan, updated 2019 , aligned with the Sendai Framework.
Institutions under the 2005 Act
The National Executive Committee (headed by the Home Secretary) assists NDMA. The National Institute of Disaster Management (NIDM) trains. The Ministry of Home Affairs is the nodal ministry.
Money and forces

Allocation follows the Finance Commission . The 15th FC (2021-26) set a framework for mitigation and capacity-building funds. States also have SDRF forces. Warning agencies: IMD (cyclone, rain), CWC (flood), INCOIS (tsunami), GSI (landslide).
The Sendai Framework, 2015-2030

Adopted in Sendai, Japan. It has four priorities : understanding risk, strengthening governance, investing in resilience, and better preparedness plus "build back better". It sets seven global targets: cut deaths, affected people, losses and raise early-warning cover. India launched the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) in 2019.
Hazard-wise mitigation

Earthquake : seismic building codes (IS 1893), retrofitting, land-use zoning. Flood : embankments, reservoirs, floodplain zoning, forecasts and ending encroachment. Cyclone : shelters, mangroves and shelter belts, early warning and evacuation. Drought : watershed work, crop planning, insurance. Landslide : slope stabilisation, hazard maps, regulating roads. Heat wave : Heat Action Plans, as in Ahmedabad (2013), now in many cities. Structural measures need money and time; non-structural ones (laws, awareness, drills) are cheaper and often more effective.
Centralised or local? "National disaster"?

The Act has no category called "national disaster"; it speaks of disasters of severe nature (L3). Kerala (2018) and Wayanad (2024) raised demands for a formal tag and more central money. Critics also say NDMA is weak in implementation and states under-use mitigation funds. Experts call for stronger local bodies and urban disaster authorities. The Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 moved in this direction. It gives statutory status to the National Crisis Management Committee, lets states raise State Disaster Response Forces, and creates Urban Disaster Management Authorities for big cities.
Success stories

Odisha cut cyclone deaths through the Odisha State Disaster Management Authority (the first in India), shelters and 10 lakh evacuations for Fani (2019). Aapda Mitra volunteers and Cyclone Mitigation Project shelters, Mission Mausam and mobile alerts (SACHET) improve warning. The failure points: urban flooding, Himalayan roads, and relief delays.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the institutional framework for disaster management in India. How far has it shifted from relief to preparedness?" (15 marks) "The Sendai Framework and India's disaster policy." (10 marks) Structure: evolution; Act and bodies; funds; Sendai; successes and gaps; suggestions (urban authorities, community role, insurance). Prelims tip: NDMA chair = Prime Minister; SDMA = CM; DDMA = Collector; the Act is 2005; NDRF came in 2006.
Map Work: India and the World
Maps earn quick marks

Prelims often gives a place name and asks you to place it. Mains rewards a sketch map or a "where is it and why does it matter" line. The cheapest marks in geography go to students who know the atlas well. Practise drawing , not just reading.
India and its neighbours
India has 7 land neighbours counting Afghanistan through PoK, and sea neighbours Sri Lanka and the Maldives. Indonesia (Great Nicobar to Aceh) and Thailand and Myanmar are close in the Andaman Sea.
Border lengths

The total land border is about 15,107 km . India's coastline is about 7,516 km (older figure). Five states touch Bangladesh: West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. West Bengal has the longest stretch.
Extremes and lines

Mainland north-south extent is about 3,214 km and east-west about 2,933 km. The Standard Meridian of 82 degrees 30 minutes E passes near Mirzapur and crosses Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. This gives a two-hour sun time gap between Arunachal and Gujarat.
States and union territories

India has 28 states and 8 union territories (as of 2025). Telangana was formed in 2014 as the 29th state of that time; J&K was split in 2019 into two UTs (J&K and Ladakh), which cut the state count to 28. The UTs are Delhi, Puducherry, J&K, Ladakh, Chandigarh, Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu (merged in 2020).
Map-reading tips for India

Learn rivers by source and mouth ; mountains by state ; passes by border ; ports by coast (east or west); national parks by state ; and cities along the Golden Quadrilateral . Make a list of "places in news" each month and mark them on a blank map.
World maps: seas and straits

Link maps to events: Ukraine war (Black Sea, Crimea, Donbas), Gaza and Red Sea (Houthi attacks on shipping from late 2023), Taiwan Strait, South China Sea ( nine-dash line , rejected by the 2016 arbitral tribunal), Sudan, and the Arctic (opening shipping routes).
Maps are political

Borders are claims. Nepal issued a new map in 2020 including Lipulekh, Kalapani and Limpiyadhura; India rejected it. China publishes "standard maps" with Arunachal and Aksai Chin. The Line of Actual Control is not marked on a common map. In answers, state India's official position and the legal basis , such as treaties, the 1914 McMahon Line or historical records.
Places in the news for India

Chabahar (Iran), Gwadar (Pakistan), Hambantota (Sri Lanka), Kyaukphyu (Myanmar), Malacca Strait , the Siliguri Corridor (Chicken's Neck), Doklam , Galwan , Great Nicobar Island and Agalega in Mauritius. Practise locating each on a sketch.
How to write this

Likely questions "Mark and label on a map of India the major ports, mountain passes and river basins." (Prelims-style or mains sketch) "Why does the Siliguri Corridor matter to India's security?" (10 marks) Structure: where it is (a line), why it matters (economic or strategic), a current link. Draw a simple sketch if the question says "map". Prelims tip: know the neighbouring country of each state; practise with an atlas every week.
